The reservoir did not dry up all at once; it exhaled. 

For three straight summers, the heat sat upon the valley like an iron skillet, baking the slate hills until they cracked and sending the sheep into the stunted shade of the gorse. Slowly, week by week, the dark blue surface of Lake Oakhaven shrank toward its deepest trench, retreating from the white-stained rim of its high-water mark. And then, in the middle of a breathless August, the drowned town of High Beck began to climb back into the daylight.

Arthur stood on the ridge, his binoculars hanging cold against his collarbone. He was sixty-eight years old, which meant he was twelve when the government men in their beige trench coats had come with clipboards and maps to explain why his grandfather’s orchard had to become the bottom of a municipal drinking basin. 

"Progress," they had called it, as though it were an incoming weather front that could neither be halted nor argued with.

Down below, the silt lay thick and gray, drying into geometric tiles that curled at the edges like dried parchment. The first thing to breach had been the spire of St. Jude’s—a weather-blackened needle of slate that had spent fifty-six years pointing at the belly of trout. Now, the roofline was bare. The nave was open to the sky again, choked with silt and long-dead freshwater weeds that looked like tangled hanks of horsehair.

Arthur adjusted his cap and started down the slope.

The walk was steep, treacherous with loose scree. His boots crunched through shale, then sank into the damp, sulfurous fringe where the lake had stood only a fortnight ago. The smell was ancient and chemical: rot, cold iron, river silt, and the faint, sweet decay of waterlogged pine. 

Walking into High Beck felt like trespassing in a dream someone had abandoned halfway through. 

There were no roofs left on the cottages. The weight of twenty fathoms of water had long since crushed the rotting beams, dropping the slates into the parlors. But the walls remained. Local granite, mortared with lime and grit, stood waist-high, outlining the skeleton of a village. 

Arthur stopped at the crossroads. Here, the paving stones had been preserved under three feet of fine mud. He used the toe of his boot to scrape a furrow until he struck gray cobble. The sound—*clack, clack*—rang unnervingly loud in the quiet bowl of the valley.

To his left was the forge. The heavy anvil was gone, probably auctioned off in 1968 before the sluice gates were dropped, but the stone hearth remained, half-filled with gray mud that bore the webbed footprints of herons. To his right had been the post office and Mrs. Cleary’s sweetshop. Arthur stepped over the low sill of what had once been the shop door.

A rusted hoop of iron lay in the corner—the rim of a barrel. Beside it, embedded in the hardened sediment, was the bottom half of a glass bottle. He knelt down, his arthritic knees popping in the silence, and worked it free with his thumb. 

It was a codd-neck bottle, pale green and thick-walled, meant for ginger beer. Inside, instead of soda, was a small, preserved world: a handful of fine grit, three tiny bleached snail shells, and an inch of foul, trapped water that had never seen the sun. He turned it in his palm. It was remarkably heavy. Fifty years of pressure had not broken it; it had merely held it down.

Arthur set the glass gently back into its cradle of mud.

He moved farther down the lane, toward the lower meadow. This had been the lowest part of the valley, the first to drown when the river was choked with concrete. This was where his grandfather’s farm had stood: Low House.

When he reached the perimeter wall, his breath hitched. The oak tree by the gate was dead, of course—a pale, smooth sculpture of driftwood stripped of bark, its branches reaching out like fractured fingers. But the gateposts were intact. On the left post, carved deep into the limestone, were the initials *G.V.*—George Vance, his grandfather. 

Arthur reached out. The stone was cool, damp, and slick with a microscopic crust of algae, but the groove of the *G* was precisely as deep as he remembered it being when he had traced it with a grazed knuckle as a boy waiting for the milk churns to be loaded onto the dray.

He stepped into the kitchen footprint.

The flags were gone, swallowed by silt, but the cast-iron frame of the range still stood against the party wall. It was terribly rusted, swollen with flakes of orange corrosion like fungal blooms, yet the heavy latch on the oven door remained. 

Arthur remembered the morning they left. It had been raining—a cruel joke, considering the deluge that was coming. His mother had swept the floor three times, though there was no one to keep it clean for. She had left an iron kettle on the stove, lid on, clean and empty. 

He looked toward the stove now. The kettle was not there. Perhaps someone had looted it in the final days; perhaps it had floated away when the water first rose like a dark wall, lifting the lightweight things toward the surface before dropping them into the mud.

He sat on the crumbling rim of the low wall, looking out across what used to be the orchard. There were no trees left there—only a series of low, circular mounds in the silt, regular as a grid, where the stumps had slowly surrendered to the rot.

Above him, high on the hills, a logging truck geared down on the highway, its engine brake rattling like distant gunfire. It sounded thin. The real world—the modern world of fiber-optic cables, bypasses, supermarket loyalty cards, and television broadcasts—felt paper-thin compared to the silence down here. 

Down here, time hadn't moved forward; it had just been stored under pressure.

Arthur took a tin from his pocket, pulled out an old silver coin he had carried for forty years, and pressed it deep into a gap between two stones in his grandfather's kitchen wall. 

"Just in case," he whispered. To whom, he wasn't sure.

He stood up, brushed the pale gray silt from the seat of his trousers, and looked toward the dam wall a mile downstream. Clouds were gathering in the west, heavy and purple-bellied, smelling of ozone and northern rain. By tomorrow night, the downpour would hit the catchment. The streams would swell, foaming brown from the peat, and the river would pour back down into the bowl.

The drowned town would go under again. The church spire would slip beneath the ripples, the post office would disappear, and the snail shells in Mrs. Cleary’s cellar would return to the dark, undisturbed for another fifty years.

Arthur turned his back on the valley floor and began the slow climb home before the water returned.
